# Generalized Sum with Countable Non-zero Summands / Corollary

## 0. The statement, and a reading of it

Throughout, $V$ is a Banach space over $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ with norm $\norm{\,\cdot\,}$,
$(v_i)_{i \in I}$ is an indexed family in $V$, and
$$S \;:=\; \set{i \in I : v_i \ne 0}$$
is its **support**. We are given countably infinite sets $J, K \subseteq I$ with $S \subseteq J \cap K$,
enumerations of $J$ and of $K$, and a number $r \in \mathbb R_{>0}$; the assertion to be proved is that
the series along the enumeration of $J$ "converges absolutely to $r$" iff the series along the
enumeration of $K$ does.

Two points of the formulation must be fixed before anything can be proved.

**(a) What "converges absolutely to $r$" means.**  The partial sums of $\sum_n v_{j_n}$ lie in $V$,
whereas $r$ is a *positive real number*; so the value $r$ cannot in general be the vector sum of the
series.  The reading forced by the hypothesis $r \in \mathbb R_{>0}$ is the one attached to the notion
of absolute convergence itself:
$$\text{"}\textstyle\sum_n v_{j_n}\text{ converges absolutely to } r\text{"}
\quad:\Longleftrightarrow\quad \sum_n \norm{v_{j_n}} \text{ converges, with } \sum_n \norm{v_{j_n}} = r .$$
This is Reading 1. For completeness we also prove the statement under

Reading 2: "$\sum_n v_{j_n}$ converges absolutely and its **vector** sum equals $w$", for a prescribed
$w \in V$ (this is the meaningful vector-valued variant; it specialises to the literal text when
$V \supseteq \mathbb R$ and $w = r$).

Theorem A below establishes the equivalence under *both* readings simultaneously.  We stress that
the two readings are genuinely different and are **not** mixed anywhere in the proof: from
$\sum_n\norm{v_{j_n}} = r$ one may *not* infer $\sum_n v_{j_n} = r$ (already for $I=\mathbb N$,
$V=\mathbb R$, $v_0=-1$, $v_n=0$ $(n\ge1)$ one has $\sum\abs{v_n}=1$ but $\sum v_n=-1$).

**(b) An indexing inconsistency.**  The enumerations are written $\set{j_0, j_1, j_2, \dots}$ and
$\set{k_0,k_1,k_2,\dots}$, i.e. they are indexed by $\mathbb N = \set{0,1,2,\dots}$, while the series
displayed are $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} v_{j_n}$ and $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} v_{k_n}$, which **omit the terms
$v_{j_0}$ and $v_{k_0}$**.  Taken literally (enumerations starting at index $0$, summation starting at
$n=1$) the stated equivalence is **false**; this is proved in Proposition B, which exhibits a
counterexample.  The defect is purely the off-by-one: as soon as the summation range and the
enumeration range agree — i.e. for the series $\sum_{n=0}^\infty v_{j_n}$ over the given
enumerations, or equivalently for $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} v_{j_n}$ when the enumerations are written
$\set{j_1,j_2,j_3,\dots}$ as the displayed series suggests — the assertion is true, and this is the
content of Theorem A.  So the claim is correct as intended and false only as literally punctuated;
we prove the corrected version in full and then prove the failure of the literal version.

**Conventions.** $\mathbb N = \set{0,1,2,\dots}$.  An *enumeration* of a countably infinite set $A$ is a
bijection $\alpha : \mathbb N \to A$; we write $a_n := \alpha(n)$, so that $A = \set{a_0,a_1,a_2,\dots}$
with the $a_n$ pairwise distinct.  For a finite set $F$ and a map $g$ into $V$ or into
$[0,\infty]$, $\sum_{i \in F} g(i)$ denotes the (order-independent, by commutativity and
associativity of addition) finite sum, with $\sum_{i\in\emptyset} g(i) = 0$.  Suprema are taken in
$[0,\infty]$.

## 1. Unordered sums of non-negative terms

**Definition.** For a set $A$ and $f : A \to [0,\infty)$ put
$$\Sigma_A f \;:=\; \sup\set[\Big]{ \sum_{i \in F} f(i) \;:\; F \subseteq A \text{ finite} } \;\in\; [0,\infty] .$$
(For $A$ countable this is exactly the *generalized sum* of $(f(i))_{i\in A}$, i.e. the limit of the
net $F \mapsto \sum_{i\in F} f(i)$ over the finite subsets of $A$ directed by inclusion, whenever that
net converges; monotonicity in $F$ makes the net convergent precisely when $\Sigma_A f < \infty$, with
limit $\Sigma_A f$. We shall not need this reformulation, but it is the link to the parent theorem.)

**Lemma 1 (every enumeration computes $\Sigma_A f$).**
*Let $A$ be countably infinite, let $f : A \to [0,\infty)$, and let $\alpha : \mathbb N \to A$,
$a_n = \alpha(n)$, be an enumeration of $A$.  Then the partial sums
$T_N := \sum_{n=0}^{N} f(a_n)$ form a non-decreasing sequence and*
$$\lim_{N \to \infty} T_N \;=\; \sup_{N \in \mathbb N} T_N \;=\; \Sigma_A f \qquad\text{in } [0,\infty] .$$
*In particular $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} f(a_n)$ converges in $\mathbb R$ iff $\Sigma_A f < \infty$, and then
its value is $\Sigma_A f$; consequently this value does not depend on the chosen enumeration.*

*Proof.* Since $f \ge 0$ we have $T_{N+1} - T_N = f(a_{N+1}) \ge 0$, so $(T_N)$ is non-decreasing and
hence converges in $[0,\infty]$ to $L := \sup_N T_N$ (by the monotone convergence theorem for
sequences of reals: if $L<\infty$ the sequence converges to $L$; if $L=\infty$ it diverges to
$+\infty$).

$L \le \Sigma_A f$: the set $F_N := \set{a_0,\dots,a_N}$ is a finite subset of $A$ and, the $a_n$ being
pairwise distinct, $T_N = \sum_{i \in F_N} f(i) \le \Sigma_A f$.  Taking the supremum over $N$ gives
$L \le \Sigma_A f$.

$\Sigma_A f \le L$: let $F \subseteq A$ be finite.  As $\alpha$ is a bijection, $\alpha^{-1}(F)$ is a
finite subset of $\mathbb N$; put $N := \max \alpha^{-1}(F)$ if $F \ne \emptyset$ and $N := 0$
otherwise.  Then $F \subseteq F_N$, and since $f \ge 0$,
$\sum_{i \in F} f(i) \le \sum_{i \in F_N} f(i) = T_N \le L$.  Taking the supremum over all finite
$F \subseteq A$ gives $\Sigma_A f \le L$.

Hence $L = \Sigma_A f$.  The final statements are immediate, because a non-decreasing real sequence
converges iff its supremum is finite, and $\Sigma_A f$ was defined without reference to $\alpha$.
$\blacksquare$

**Lemma 2 (terms equal to $0$ may be discarded).**
*Let $B \subseteq A$ and let $f : A \to [0,\infty)$ satisfy $f(i) = 0$ for all $i \in A \setminus B$.
Then $\Sigma_A f = \Sigma_B (f|_B)$.*

*Proof.* Every finite $F \subseteq B$ is a finite subset of $A$ with the same sum, so
$\Sigma_B(f|_B) \le \Sigma_A f$.  Conversely, let $F \subseteq A$ be finite.  Then $F \cap B$ is a
finite subset of $B$ and, since $f$ vanishes on $F \setminus B \subseteq A\setminus B$,
$$\sum_{i \in F} f(i) = \sum_{i \in F \cap B} f(i) + \sum_{i \in F \setminus B} f(i)
= \sum_{i \in F \cap B} f(i) \le \Sigma_B (f|_B) .$$
Taking the supremum over $F$ gives $\Sigma_A f \le \Sigma_B(f|_B)$.  (No countability or infinitude
assumption on $A$ or $B$ is used.) $\blacksquare$

**Lemma 3 (small tails).**
*Let $f : A \to [0,\infty)$ with $\Sigma_A f = c < \infty$, and let $\varepsilon > 0$.  Then there is a
finite $F \subseteq A$ such that $\sum_{i \in G} f(i) < \varepsilon$ for every finite
$G \subseteq A \setminus F$.*

*Proof.* By definition of the supremum there is a finite $F \subseteq A$ with
$\sum_{i \in F} f(i) > c - \varepsilon$ (the sup is over a non-empty family, as $F=\emptyset$ is
allowed, and $c<\infty$).  Let $G \subseteq A \setminus F$ be finite.  Then $F \cup G$ is finite and
$F \cap G = \emptyset$, so
$$\sum_{i \in F} f(i) + \sum_{i \in G} f(i) = \sum_{i \in F \cup G} f(i) \le \Sigma_A f = c ,$$
whence $\sum_{i\in G} f(i) \le c - \sum_{i \in F} f(i) < \varepsilon$. $\blacksquare$

## 2. The theorem

Recall $S = \set{i \in I : v_i \ne 0}$ and define
$$f : I \to [0,\infty), \qquad f(i) := \norm{v_i} .$$
By the positivity axiom of a norm, $f(i) = 0 \iff v_i = 0 \iff i \notin S$; i.e. **$f$ vanishes exactly
off $S$**.

**Theorem A.** *Let $V$ be a Banach space, $(v_i)_{i\in I}$ a family in $V$, and let $J,K \subseteq I$ be
countably infinite with $S \subseteq J \cap K$.  Let $(j_n)_{n \in \mathbb N}$ and
$(k_n)_{n \in \mathbb N}$ enumerate $J$ and $K$ respectively.  Then:*

1. *(Equality of norm-sums.)*
 $$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \norm{v_{j_n}} \;=\; \Sigma_S f \;=\; \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \norm{v_{k_n}}
 \qquad \text{as elements of } [0,\infty] ,$$
 *both series of non-negative reals having monotone partial sums.  In particular
 $\sum_{n \ge 0} v_{j_n}$ is absolutely convergent iff $\sum_{n\ge0} v_{k_n}$ is, and in that case the
 two sums of norms are equal.*
2. *(Equality of vector sums.)*  *If these series are absolutely convergent then both
 $\sum_{n=0}^\infty v_{j_n}$ and $\sum_{n=0}^\infty v_{k_n}$ converge in $V$ and*
 $$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} v_{j_n} \;=\; \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} v_{k_n} .$$
3. *Consequently, for every $r \in [0,\infty)$ — in particular for every $r \in \mathbb R_{>0}$ —*
 $$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} v_{j_n} \text{ converges absolutely with } \sum_{n=0}^\infty \norm{v_{j_n}} = r
 \iff \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} v_{k_n} \text{ converges absolutely with } \sum_{n=0}^\infty \norm{v_{k_n}} = r,$$
 *and for every $w \in V$*
 $$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} v_{j_n} \text{ converges absolutely with sum } w
 \iff \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} v_{k_n} \text{ converges absolutely with sum } w .$$

*Proof.*

**(1).** Apply Lemma 1 to the countably infinite set $A = J$, the function $f|_J \ge 0$ and the
enumeration $(j_n)$:
$$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \norm{v_{j_n}} \;=\; \lim_{N\to\infty}\sum_{n=0}^{N} f(j_n) \;=\; \Sigma_J (f|_J) .$$
Now $S \subseteq J$ by hypothesis, and $f$ vanishes on $J \setminus S$ (indeed off $S$ altogether), so
Lemma 2 with $A = J$, $B = S$ gives $\Sigma_J(f|_J) = \Sigma_S(f|_S) = \Sigma_S f$.  Hence
$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\norm{v_{j_n}} = \Sigma_S f$.  The identical argument with $K$ (which is countably
infinite and contains $S$) and the enumeration $(k_n)$ gives
$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\norm{v_{k_n}} = \Sigma_S f$.  Since $\Sigma_S f$ is one and the same element of
$[0,\infty]$, the two monotone limits coincide; and a series of non-negative reals converges iff its
monotone limit is finite, so one of $\sum_n \norm{v_{j_n}}$, $\sum_n \norm{v_{k_n}}$ converges iff the
other does (namely iff $\Sigma_S f < \infty$), with the same value.  By definition, absolute
convergence of $\sum_n v_{j_n}$ *is* convergence of $\sum_n \norm{v_{j_n}}$. This proves (1).

**(2).** Assume absolute convergence, and set $c := \Sigma_S f < \infty$ by (1).

*Convergence in $V$.*  Let $P_N := \sum_{n=0}^{N} v_{j_n}$.  For $M > N$, the triangle inequality gives
$$\norm{P_M - P_N} = \Bignorm{\sum_{n=N+1}^{M} v_{j_n}} \le \sum_{n=N+1}^{M} \norm{v_{j_n}} = T_M - T_N,$$
where $T_N = \sum_{n=0}^N \norm{v_{j_n}}$.  As $(T_N)$ converges, it is Cauchy, so
$(P_N)$ is a Cauchy sequence in $V$; $V$ being complete, $P_N \to L_J$ for some $L_J \in V$, i.e.
$\sum_{n=0}^\infty v_{j_n} = L_J$.  Likewise $Q_N := \sum_{n=0}^N v_{k_n} \to L_K =: \sum_{n=0}^\infty v_{k_n}$.

*Equality.*  Let $\varepsilon > 0$.  Apply Lemma 3 to $f|_S$ on $A = S$ (legitimate: $\Sigma_S f = c <
\infty$): there is a finite $F \subseteq S$ with
$$\sum_{i \in G} \norm{v_i} < \varepsilon \qquad \text{for every finite } G \subseteq S \setminus F. \tag{$*$}$$
Put $u := \sum_{i \in F} v_i \in V$.  Since $F \subseteq S \subseteq J$ is finite and $n \mapsto j_n$ is a
bijection $\mathbb N \to J$, the set $\set{n \in \mathbb N : j_n \in F}$ is finite; let $N_0$ be its
maximum (or $N_0 := 0$ if $F = \emptyset$), so that
$F \subseteq \set{j_0,\dots,j_{N}}$ for all $N \ge N_0$.  Fix such an $N$ and write
$F_N := \set{j_0,\dots,j_N}$, a set of $N+1$ distinct elements of $J$ with $F \subseteq F_N$.  Then
$$P_N - u = \sum_{i \in F_N} v_i - \sum_{i \in F} v_i = \sum_{i \in F_N \setminus F} v_i ,$$
and since $v_i = 0$ for $i \notin S$,
$$\norm{P_N - u} \le \sum_{i \in F_N \setminus F} \norm{v_i} = \sum_{i \in G_N} \norm{v_i}, \qquad
G_N := (F_N \cap S) \setminus F .$$
Now $G_N$ is a finite subset of $S \setminus F$, so $(*)$ gives $\norm{P_N - u} < \varepsilon$ for all
$N \ge N_0$.  Letting $N \to \infty$ and using continuity of the norm,
$\norm{L_J - u} \le \varepsilon$.  The same argument applied to $K$ (using $F \subseteq S \subseteq K$)
yields $\norm{L_K - u} \le \varepsilon$.  Hence
$$\norm{L_J - L_K} \le \norm{L_J - u} + \norm{u - L_K} \le 2\varepsilon .$$
As $\varepsilon > 0$ was arbitrary, $\norm{L_J - L_K} = 0$, i.e. $L_J = L_K$.

**(3).** The first equivalence is immediate from (1): both sides say
"$\Sigma_S f < \infty$ and $\Sigma_S f = r$", i.e. "$\Sigma_S f = r$".  For the second, suppose
$\sum_{n\ge0} v_{j_n}$ converges absolutely with sum $w$.  By (1), $\sum_{n\ge0} v_{k_n}$ converges
absolutely, and by (2) its sum equals $\sum_{n\ge0} v_{j_n} = w$.  The converse follows by
interchanging the roles of $(J,(j_n))$ and $(K,(k_n))$, the hypotheses being symmetric in them.
$\blacksquare$

**Remarks.**

* The hypothesis $r > 0$ is never used: the equivalence holds for every $r \in [0,\infty)$, and also
 in the degenerate direction, since by (1) the two norm-series diverge together.
* The hypothesis $S \subseteq J \cap K$ is exactly what is needed.  It cannot be dropped: with
 $I = \mathbb N$, $V = \mathbb R$, $v_0 = 1$ and $v_n = 0$ for $n \ge 1$, take
 $J = \mathbb N$ and $K = \set{1,2,3,\dots}$ (both countably infinite) with the increasing
 enumerations.  Then $\sum_{n\ge0}\abs{v_{j_n}} = 1$ while $\sum_{n \ge 0}\abs{v_{k_n}} = 0$: the
 equivalence fails for $r = 1$, and indeed $S = \set0 \not\subseteq K$.
* Neither $J$ nor $K$ need be related to the other beyond containing $S$; they may be disjoint outside
 $S$, and $S$ itself may be finite or empty.  Both sides are equal to the enumeration-free quantity
 $\Sigma_S f$, which is the generalized (net) sum of $(\norm{v_i})_{i \in S}$ — equivalently of
 $(\norm{v_i})_{i\in I}$, by Lemma 2 with $A = I$, $B = S$.  This is why the corollary follows from the
 parent theorem "Generalized Sum with Countable Non-zero Summands": each side is equivalent to the
 single statement $\Sigma_I f = r$, and equivalence to a common statement is transitive.
* Completeness of $V$ is used only in part (2), to produce the vector sums; part (1) and the first
 equivalence in (3) hold in any normed vector space.

## 3. The literal reading is false

**Proposition B.** *Read literally — enumerations indexed as $\set{j_0,j_1,j_2,\dots}$,
$\set{k_0,k_1,k_2,\dots}$ but series summed from $n = 1$ — the stated equivalence fails.*

*Proof.* Take $V = \mathbb R$ (a Banach space with $\norm x = \abs x$), $I = \mathbb N$, and
$$v_0 := 1, \qquad v_n := 0 \quad (n \ge 1) .$$
Then $S = \set{i \in I : v_i \ne 0} = \set 0$.  Take $J = K = \mathbb N$, which are countably infinite
subsets of $I$ with $S = \set0 \subseteq J \cap K = \mathbb N$.  All hypotheses hold.  Let $r := 1 \in
\mathbb R_{>0}$.  Choose the enumerations
$$j_n := n \quad (n \ge 0); \qquad k_0 := 1,\quad k_1 := 0,\quad k_n := n \ \ (n \ge 2) .$$
Both are bijections $\mathbb N \to \mathbb N$: the first is the identity, and the second is the identity
composed with the transposition of $0$ and $1$.  Now
$$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} v_{j_n} = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} v_n = 0 , \qquad
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \abs{v_{j_n}} = 0 ,$$
so $\sum_{n=1}^\infty v_{j_n}$ converges absolutely, but with norm-sum $0 \ne 1 = r$ and vector sum
$0 \ne r$: under either reading it does **not** converge absolutely *to $r$*.  On the other hand
$$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} v_{k_n} = v_{k_1} + \sum_{n=2}^\infty v_n = v_0 + 0 = 1 , \qquad
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \abs{v_{k_n}} = \abs{v_0} = 1 = r ,$$
so $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} v_{k_n}$ does converge absolutely to $r$ under either reading.  Hence the
right-hand side of the claimed equivalence holds while the left-hand side fails, and the equivalence
is false as literally stated. $\blacksquare$

The mechanism is transparent: summing from $n=1$ while enumerating from index $0$ silently deletes the
term $v_{j_0}$, and since an enumeration may place *any* prescribed element of $J$ in slot $0$, the
deleted term can be made to carry all of the mass for one enumeration and none of it for another.
Once the summation range matches the enumeration range — $\sum_{n=0}^\infty$ over
$\set{j_0,j_1,\dots}$, or equivalently $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}$ over $\set{j_1,j_2,\dots}$ (replace
$\mathbb N$ by $\mathbb Z_{\ge 1}$ throughout Lemma 1, which uses nothing about $\mathbb N$ beyond its
being the index set of the enumeration) — Theorem A applies and the equivalence is true.

## 4. Conclusion

With "converges absolutely to $r$" meaning $\sum_n \norm{v_{j_n}} = r$ (Reading 1) or meaning
"absolutely convergent with vector sum $r$" (Reading 2), and with the series taken over the *whole*
given enumeration, the assertion is true: by Theorem A(1) both norm-series have the common value
$\Sigma_S \norm{v_\cdot} \in [0,\infty]$, so they converge absolutely together and to the same value,
and by Theorem A(2) the vector sums then agree as well.  Taken with its literal off-by-one
(enumeration from index $0$, summation from $n = 1$), the assertion is false, by the counterexample of
Proposition B.
